title: Rome falls (410)
hook: the city is sacked, and Augustine writes City of God: two cities, two loves

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ostia, and your line was at the window. Who did you sit with, and what did you ask them? Day seven hundred eighty-one.

The news crosses the sea, and it's hard to believe. Rome has been sacked. An army of Goths has broken into the city and plundered it. People who fled are arriving. And some are saying out loud what they're thinking: this happened because Rome turned from its old gods to the Christian one. Across the water in Africa, Augustine is now a bishop. He hears the charge. He picks up his pen to answer it, and the answer grows into a very long book. Today: Rome falls.
screen: `THE OLD GODS, OR THE NEW ONE?`

segments.voice: The book is The City of God. Augustine starts with the charge itself. During the sack, he points out, the invaders spared people who fled into the churches of the apostles, and some of those spared are now the ones blaming Christ. Then he goes much further than a reply. There are, he says, two cities mixed together in this world. Not two places. Two loves. The Psalms sing of one of them, in the King James words: "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God." Beside it Augustine sets the earthly city. And then comes the line that holds the whole book together. Two loves, he writes, have made two cities. Love of self, reaching even to contempt of God, made the earthly city. Love of God, reaching even to contempt of self, made the heavenly one. That changes the question. For Augustine, Rome was never the city of God, not even a Christian Rome. No empire is. The two cities run through every street and every church, tangled together until the end. So when Rome falls, he tells his readers, they may grieve, but their hope was not built on its walls. The letter to the Hebrews had already said it: "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come." That's no excuse to stop caring about the earthly city. Augustine says the heavenly city, while it's on pilgrimage here, makes use of the earthly city's peace and seeks it, since its people share that life too. But it puts every city, every party, every institution under the same question: what does it love? And the question doesn't stop at the city limits. It runs through each person, too.
screen: `NO EMPIRE IS THE CITY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask which city you're building. Settle, and breathe. Think of the places your days go into: your work, your home, a group you belong to, the screen in your pocket. Pick one. Then ask Augustine's question of it, quietly. What is it built on? What does it love? And what am I adding to it: love that curls inward, or love that turns outward? Don't grade yourself. Just look. If you pray, you can offer that place to God. If you don't, simply see it clearly for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Rome falls. The sack of the city that set Augustine writing The City of God: two cities, made by two loves, mixed until the end.
Your line: two cities, two loves. Today, before you give an hour to something, ask which city it builds. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Augustine's City of God is read and taught by Christians of different churches, especially when they think about faith and public life; his image of two cities and two loves is often cited in that conversation.

fork.setup: you're a bishop. people who fled Rome are arriving, and some say the city fell because it abandoned its old gods. what do you do?
options: say nothing: the talk will pass.
answer the charge, then write about two cities and two loves.
say God punished Rome, and leave it there.
fork.reveal: Augustine answered, and kept going. his reply became The City of God: no empire is God's city; two loves build two cities.

original.note: Greek: city. the word behind here have we no continuing city, in Hebrews.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rome fell, so the church took over.
what it means: when Rome was sacked, Augustine answered that no earthly city, even a Christian one, is the city of God. two loves build two cities.
what a scholar hears: the two cities are mixed until the end, and the heavenly city, on pilgrimage, still makes use of the earthly city's peace.

notes: No year is spoken (the index title carries 410). The Goths are named; Alaric is not. Confirm 'people who fled are arriving with nothing' (refugees to Africa are attested in Augustine's sermons and letters, not cited here).
City of God 1.1 and 1.7: the barbarians spared those who fled to the basilicas of the apostles, including some now blaming Christ. Paraphrased; confirm.
City of God 14.28: 'two loves have formed two cities' paraphrased (Dods 1871 is not on the public-domain list used here).
City of God 19.17: the heavenly city on pilgrimage makes use of the earthly peace. Confirm paraphrase.
Not stated: how long Augustine took or how many books the work has (claims rule). 'A very long book' is a soft description; confirm.

Editor: 'nobody wants to believe it' softened; the claims that no empire is the city of God and that Christians' hope was not built on Rome are now attributed to Augustine, not stated by the narrator.
